question: What type of bond is formed when electrons are shared between two non-metal atoms?
What happens to electrons during the formation of an ionic bond?
options: Electrons are transferred from non-metal to metal
Electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal
correct: Electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal

question: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
options: They have strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
They are made of large molecules
correct: They have strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions

question: When can ionic compounds conduct electricity?
options: When dissolved in water or melted
correct: When dissolved in water or melted

question: Why do simple molecular substances have low melting points?
options: They have weak intermolecular forces between molecules
correct: They have weak intermolecular forces between molecules

question: Which of the following is a giant covalent structure?
Why can graphite conduct electricity but diamond cannot?
options: Graphite has delocalised electrons that are free to move
Diamond is a gas at room temperature
correct: Graphite has delocalised electrons that are free to move

question: What is the structure of a metal?
options: Giant lattice of positive ions with delocalised electrons
correct: Giant lattice of positive ions with delocalised electrons

question: Why are alloys harder than pure metals?
options: Different sized atoms distort the lattice, making it harder for layers to slide
correct: Different sized atoms distort the lattice, making it harder for layers to slide

question: Which statement about fullerenes is correct?
options: They are made of silicon atoms
They are hollow molecules made of carbon atoms
correct: They are hollow molecules made of carbon atoms

question: What is the size range of nanoparticles?
Why do nanoparticles have different properties to the same material in bulk?
options: They have a different chemical formula
They have a much larger surface area to volume ratio
correct: They have a much larger surface area to volume ratio

question: What is a polymer?
options: A small molecule that joins to form chains
A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units
correct: A large molecule made of many repeating monomer units

question: What is graphene?
options: A single layer of graphite one atom thick
A type of fullerene shaped like a sphere
correct: A single layer of graphite one atom thick

question: Which type of bonding is found in metals?
In ionic bonding, electrons are __________ from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
In covalent bonding, atoms __________ a pair of electrons.
Ionic compounds are arranged in a giant __________ lattice.
Diamond and graphite are both forms of the element __________.
Metals conduct electricity because they have __________ electrons that are free to move.
An __________ is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, making it harder than the pure metal.
Simple molecular substances have __________ melting points because of weak intermolecular forces.
Buckminsterfullerene has the chemical formula __________.
Nanoparticles have a very large __________ area to volume ratio.
The small repeating units that join together to make a polymer are called __________.
Match each type of bonding to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Electrons transferred from metal to non-metal — forms oppositely charged ions
Positive ions in a lattice surrounded by delocalised electrons

question: Match each form of carbon to its key property.

pairs.definition: Very hard, high melting point, does not conduct electricity
Soft and slippery, conducts electricity due to delocalised electrons
Single layer of carbon atoms — very strong and excellent conductor
Hollow sphere of 60 carbon atoms — used in drug delivery

question: Match each structure type to its melting point and conductivity.

pairs.definition: High melting point — does not conduct electricity when solid
Low melting point — does not conduct electricity
Variable melting point — conducts electricity in all states
Very high melting point — usually does not conduct electricity

question: Match each term to its correct definition.

pairs.definition: Small molecule that joins with others to form a polymer
Large molecule made of many repeating monomer units
Mixture of a metal with other elements — harder than pure metal
Electron free to move throughout a metallic structure

question: Match each nanotechnology term to its correct description.

pairs.definition: Particle between 1 and 100 nm in size with a large surface area to volume ratio
Cylindrical carbon fullerene with high strength and electrical conductivity
Unit of measurement equal to 1 × 10⁻⁹ m

question: State what is meant by a covalent bond.
mark_scheme: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms (1).

question: State one condition under which an ionic compound can conduct electricity.
mark_scheme: When dissolved in water (aqueous solution) (1) / when melted (molten) (1).

question: State why simple molecular compounds do not conduct electricity.
mark_scheme: They have no free electrons / no ions to carry charge (1).

question: State why metals are good conductors of electricity.
mark_scheme: They have delocalised electrons that are free to move and carry charge (1).

question: Explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
mark_scheme: Ionic compounds have a giant lattice structure (1); with strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions that require a lot of energy to break (1).

question: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
mark_scheme: Diamond has a giant covalent structure (1); with many strong covalent bonds that require a lot of energy to break (1).

question: Explain why metals are malleable.
mark_scheme: Layers of ions in a metal can slide over each other (1); the delocalised electrons hold the structure together even when layers move (1).

question: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals.
mark_scheme: Alloys contain atoms of different sizes (1); these disrupt the regular lattice, making it harder for layers to slide over each other (1).

question: Describe the structure of graphite and explain why it can conduct electricity.
mark_scheme: Carbon atoms are arranged in layers (1); each atom bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom that is free to carry charge (1).

question: State two uses of nanoparticles.
mark_scheme: Any two from: sun cream (1); antibacterial coatings (1); drug delivery (1); catalysts (1); electronics (1).

question: Explain what happens to electrons when sodium and chlorine react to form sodium chloride.
mark_scheme: The sodium atom loses one electron (1); the chlorine atom gains one electron (1); forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by electrostatic attraction (1) — any two.

question: Compare the structures of diamond and graphite.
mark_scheme: Both have giant covalent structures / both made of carbon (1); diamond has each carbon bonded to four others in a 3D lattice; graphite has layers of carbon atoms each bonded to three others (1).

question: Explain why simple molecular substances have low melting and boiling points, even though their covalent bonds are strong.
mark_scheme: Simple molecules have strong covalent bonds within the molecule (1); but only weak intermolecular forces between molecules (1); it is the intermolecular forces that are broken during melting/boiling, not the covalent bonds, so little energy is needed (1).

question: Explain why nanoparticles may have different properties from the same material in bulk form.
mark_scheme: Nanoparticles are very small (1–100 nm) (1); they have a much larger surface area to volume ratio (1); this means more atoms are on the surface, changing their chemical and physical properties (1).

question: Describe the three types of strong chemical bonding. State which types of elements are involved in each.
mark_scheme: Ionic: metal transfers electrons to non-metal, forming ions (1); covalent: non-metals share electrons (1); metallic: metal ions in a lattice with delocalised electrons (1).

question: Explain the structure and bonding in sodium chloride and use this to explain its properties.
mark_scheme: Giant ionic lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (1); held together by strong electrostatic attraction (1); high melting point because a lot of energy is needed to break these forces (1); conducts electricity when molten or dissolved because ions are free to move (1).

question: Compare the structures and properties of diamond and graphite. Explain why their properties differ despite both being made of carbon.
mark_scheme: Diamond: each carbon bonded to four others, giant 3D lattice, very hard, high melting point, no free electrons so does not conduct (1); graphite: each carbon bonded to three others in layers, layers slide so it is soft, has delocalised electrons so conducts electricity (1); differences in properties arise from different bonding arrangements / structures (1); both have giant covalent structures with high melting points (1).

question: Explain the structure and bonding in metals and use this to explain why metals are good conductors of electricity and heat, and why they are malleable.
mark_scheme: Giant lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalised electrons (1); delocalised electrons carry charge so metals conduct electricity (1); delocalised electrons transfer energy so metals conduct heat (1); layers of ions can slide without breaking bonds — metals are malleable (1).

question: Evaluate the use of nanoparticles in everyday products. Include potential benefits and risks in your answer.
mark_scheme: Benefits: large surface area makes them effective catalysts (1); used in sunscreens, antibacterial products, drug delivery systems (1); can target cancer cells specifically / more effective than bulk materials (1); risks: potential toxicity to human cells / unknown long-term health effects (1); may accumulate in environment / organisms (1) — any four.

question: Explain the structures and properties of fullerenes and nanotubes. Include their uses in your answer.
mark_scheme: Fullerenes are hollow molecules made of carbon atoms arranged in rings (1); buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) is a spherical example (1); nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high tensile strength (1); both have delocalised electrons so can conduct electricity (1); uses: drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts, electronics, reinforcing materials (1).

question: A student tests four substances to find out which conducts electricity and measures their melting points. Substance A melts at 801°C and conducts when dissolved. Substance B melts at 3550°C and never conducts. Substance C melts at –114°C and never conducts. Substance D melts at 1085°C and always conducts. Identify the type of structure of each substance and justify your answers.
mark_scheme: Substance A: ionic compound — high melting point and conducts when dissolved (ions free to move) (1); substance B: giant covalent structure — very high melting point and never conducts (no free electrons/ions) (1); substance C: simple molecular — very low melting point (weak intermolecular forces) and never conducts (1); substance D: metal — high melting point and always conducts (delocalised electrons) (1); full justifications referencing bonding/structure for each (1); clear reasoning linking evidence to conclusion (1).

question: Explain how ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds are formed and compare the properties of substances with each type of bonding. Use examples in your answer.
mark_scheme: Ionic: electrons transferred from metal to non-metal — forms ions attracted by electrostatic forces e.g. NaCl — high mp, conducts when molten/dissolved (1); covalent: electrons shared between non-metals e.g. H₂O — simple molecules have low mp / giant covalent has very high mp, generally poor conductors (1); metallic: delocalised electrons in lattice of positive ions e.g. copper — conducts electricity and heat, malleable, variable mp (1); ionic and metallic have giant structures with high melting points; simple molecules have low melting points (1); only metals and graphite conduct as solids (1); ionic compounds only conduct when ions are free to move (1).

question: Explain the difference between ionic and covalent bonding. Include which types of elements form each and the particles involved.
mark_scheme: Ionic bonding: between a metal and a non-metal — electrons transferred from metal to non-metal (1); metal loses electrons to form positive ion; non-metal gains electrons to form negative ion (1); covalent bonding: between two non-metals — electrons shared between atoms (1); both atoms achieve a full outer shell through sharing (1).

question: Describe the structure of an ionic compound and explain why ionic compounds have high melting points.
mark_scheme: Ionic compounds form a giant ionic lattice — regular arrangement of positive and negative ions (1); held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions (1); high melting points because a large amount of energy needed to overcome these strong forces (1); melting requires breaking many ionic bonds throughout the whole lattice (1).

question: Explain why simple molecular covalent substances (e.g. water, oxygen) have low boiling points, while giant covalent structures (e.g. diamond) have very high boiling points.
mark_scheme: Simple molecular: held together by weak intermolecular forces between molecules (1); little energy needed to overcome these — low boiling point (1); giant covalent: atoms joined by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure (1); very large amount of energy needed to break all bonds — very high melting/boiling point (1).

question: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity and heat. Include the term 'delocalised electrons' in your answer.
mark_scheme: Metals have a giant metallic lattice structure — positive ions in a regular arrangement (1); outer electrons are delocalised — free to move throughout the structure (1); delocalised electrons carry electrical charge — conduct electricity (1); delocalised electrons also transfer kinetic energy — conduct heat (1).

question: Describe the structure and properties of graphite and explain why it is used as a lubricant and as an electrode.
mark_scheme: Graphite: layers of carbon atoms in hexagonal rings — each carbon bonded to three others (1); layers held by weak intermolecular forces — can slide over each other easily (1); lubricant: layers slide — reduces friction between surfaces (1); electrode: one delocalised electron per carbon atom — free to move along layers — conducts electricity (1).

question: Explain why ionic compounds conduct electricity when dissolved in water or melted, but not when solid.
mark_scheme: When solid: ions held in fixed positions in the lattice — cannot move to carry charge (1); when dissolved in water: lattice breaks down, ions separate and are free to move (1); when melted: ions gain enough energy to break free from lattice — free to move (1); moving charged ions carry electrical current (1).

question: Describe how addition polymers are formed from monomers. Use poly(ethene) as an example and draw a repeat unit.
mark_scheme: Monomers contain a C=C double bond (1); under high pressure and with a catalyst, the double bond opens — monomers join together (1); long chain polymer formed — no other products (addition polymerisation) (1); repeat unit of poly(ethene): –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ– (1).

question: Explain what happens to the particles in a substance as it is heated from solid to liquid to gas. Include changes in energy and arrangement.
mark_scheme: Solid: particles vibrate in fixed positions (1); on heating: particles gain kinetic energy — vibrate more; at melting point, forces overcome — become liquid (1); liquid: particles move freely but still close together (1); at boiling point: particles gain enough energy to overcome all intermolecular forces — become gas with particles far apart and moving randomly (1).

question: Evaluate the properties of diamond and graphite as forms of carbon. Compare their structures and suggest an appropriate use for each.
mark_scheme: Diamond: each carbon bonded to 4 others in giant tetrahedral lattice — extremely hard; no delocalised electrons — does not conduct electricity (1); used as cutting tools and in drill bits (1); graphite: layers of hexagonal rings — soft and slippery; delocalised electrons — conducts electricity (1); used as lubricant and in electrodes/pencils (1).

question: Describe how to draw a dot-and-cross diagram for a covalent molecule. Use water (H₂O) as an example and show all lone pairs.
mark_scheme: Water: oxygen has 6 outer electrons, each hydrogen has 1 (1); each O–H bond: one pair of shared electrons shown between O and H (1); two lone pairs on oxygen shown (1); diagram shows all electrons in outer shells; crosses for one atom, dots for the other (1).

question: Explain why metals can be bent and shaped (malleable and ductile) without breaking. Relate this to their structure.
mark_scheme: Metals have layers of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (1); when force applied, layers of ions can slide over each other (1); delocalised electrons move with the layers — maintaining the bonding (1); unlike ionic compounds, slipping layers doesn't bring like charges together — so metal doesn't shatter (1).

question: Explain how to predict the formula of an ionic compound. Use magnesium chloride as an example and explain why ionic compounds are electrically neutral.
mark_scheme: Magnesium: Group 2 — forms Mg²⁺ ion (loses 2 electrons) (1); chlorine: Group 7 — forms Cl⁻ ion (gains 1 electron) (1); need 2 Cl⁻ to balance one Mg²⁺ — formula MgCl₂ (1); ionic compounds are neutral because total positive charge equals total negative charge (1); same principle applies to all ionic compounds — cross-charge method to find formula (1).

question: Describe the properties of fullerenes and graphene. Include their structures and suggest one potential use for each.
mark_scheme: Fullerenes: carbon atoms arranged in spheres (C₆₀ — buckminsterfullerene) or tubes (carbon nanotubes) (1); very strong and can conduct electricity — delocalised electrons (1); potential use: drug delivery — hollow cage can carry drug molecules to specific cells (1); graphene: single layer of graphite — one atom thick, hexagonal arrangement (1); extremely strong, flexible, and conducts electricity — potential use in flexible electronics / touchscreens (1).

question: Explain the differences in properties between the three states of matter using particle theory. Include compressibility, density, and ability to flow.
mark_scheme: Solids: particles in fixed, regular arrangement — incompressible, high density, cannot flow (1); liquids: particles close together but randomly arranged and can move past each other — incompressible, high density, can flow (1); gases: particles far apart and moving randomly — very compressible (1); low density compared to solid/liquid of same substance (1); gas flows easily — particles move freely in any direction; no fixed shape or volume (1).

question: Evaluate the use of polymers in everyday life. Include both addition and condensation polymers, their properties and the environmental concerns.
mark_scheme: Addition polymers: strong, cheap, waterproof — e.g. poly(ethene) in plastic bags, poly(propene) in ropes (1); condensation polymers: nylon (clothing), polyester (fabric) — can be biodegradable (1); advantages: lightweight, durable, versatile, cheap to produce (1); environmental concerns: most addition polymers non-biodegradable — persist in environment for centuries (1); plastic pollution in oceans harms wildlife; solution: recycling, bioplastics, reducing use (1).

question: Explain how the type of bonding in a substance determines its properties. Compare ionic, covalent (simple molecular) and metallic substances.
mark_scheme: Ionic: high melting point (strong lattice forces), conducts when dissolved/molten, brittle (1); simple molecular covalent: low melting point (weak intermolecular forces), does not conduct, may be soluble (1); giant covalent: very high melting point (many strong bonds to break), most do not conduct (except graphite) (1); metallic: high melting point (strong metallic bonds), good conductors, malleable and ductile (1); linking structure to properties allows us to predict and explain behaviour of unknown substances (1).

question: Describe the properties of alloys and explain why alloys are harder than pure metals. Include at least one example.
mark_scheme: Alloy: mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (1); e.g. steel: iron + carbon; bronze: copper + tin (1); in pure metal, layers of identical atoms can slide easily over each other (1); in alloy, different-sized atoms disrupt the regular arrangement (1); layers cannot slide as easily — alloy is harder and stronger than pure metal (1).

question: Explain why covalent bonds are strong but many covalent substances still have low melting points. Include intermolecular forces in your answer.
mark_scheme: Covalent bonds within molecules are strong — require large energy to break (1); but simple molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces between molecules (1); boiling/melting involves overcoming intermolecular forces — not breaking covalent bonds (1); little energy needed to separate molecules — low boiling point (1); molecules remain intact after melting/boiling — covalent bonds not broken during state changes (1).

question: Evaluate the bonding in sodium chloride, silicon dioxide and poly(ethene). Explain how the bonding determines the uses of each substance.
mark_scheme: NaCl: ionic bonding — high melting point; dissolves in water; used as table salt and in food preservation (1); SiO₂: giant covalent — very high melting point, hard, insoluble — used in glass making (1); poly(ethene): covalent, long chains — flexible, waterproof, low density — used in packaging (1); each use reflects the properties determined by bonding (1); comparing: ionic needs high temp to melt; giant covalent even harder to melt; simple molecular easily deformed (1).

question: Describe how condensation polymerisation differs from addition polymerisation. Include the monomers used, the bonds formed and a named example of each.
mark_scheme: Addition: monomers with C=C double bonds; no other products formed (1); e.g. ethene → poly(ethene) (1); condensation: two different monomers with two functional groups each (1); small molecule (water or HCl) released with each bond formed (1); e.g. nylon: diamine + dicarboxylic acid → polyamide + water (1).

question: Explain what is meant by the term 'electrostatic force' in an ionic compound. Describe the factors that affect the strength of ionic bonding.
mark_scheme: Electrostatic force: attraction between oppositely charged ions (1); ionic bond strength depends on size of charge — Mg²⁺ forms stronger bonds than Na⁺ (1); smaller ions: closer together — stronger attraction (1); higher charge density = stronger ionic bond = higher melting point (1); e.g. MgO melts at 2852°C vs NaCl at 801°C — Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ both 2+ charges vs 1+ and 1− (1).

question: Explain the bonding and structure of diamond, graphite and graphene. For each, relate the structure to at least one specific property and use.
mark_scheme: Diamond: each C atom forms 4 covalent bonds — giant covalent tetrahedral lattice (1); extremely hard — used in cutting tools; very high melting point; no free electrons — does not conduct (1); graphite: each C forms 3 bonds — hexagonal layers (1); layers held by weak forces — can slide; one free electron per C — conducts electricity; used as lubricant and electrode (1); graphene: single layer of graphite — one atom thick (1); incredibly strong per unit mass, flexible and transparent — potential for flexible electronics, composites; conducts electricity (1).

question: Evaluate the environmental impact of synthetic polymers. Include how they are produced, why they are difficult to dispose of, and methods to reduce their impact.
mark_scheme: Most synthetic polymers made from crude oil — non-renewable resource (1); non-biodegradable — persist for hundreds of years in landfill and oceans (1); microplastics break off and enter food chains — harmful to wildlife (1); incineration releases CO₂ and toxic gases (1); recycling: reduces landfill and resource use but requires sorting; not all types recyclable (1); bioplastics: made from plant starch — biodegradable; but require land use to grow crops (1).

question: Describe the changes of state that occur when water is heated from −20°C to 120°C. Include what is happening to particles, energy, and bonds at each stage.
mark_scheme: −20°C to 0°C: solid ice — particles vibrate; temperature rises as KE increases (1); at 0°C (melting point): temperature stays constant — energy breaks intermolecular forces in lattice; solid → liquid (1); 0–100°C: liquid water — particles move freely; temperature rises (1); at 100°C (boiling point): temperature constant — energy overcomes intermolecular forces between water molecules; liquid → gas (1); above 100°C: steam — particles move rapidly and independently (1); covalent O–H bonds within water molecules NOT broken at any stage — only intermolecular forces change (1).

question: Explain why sodium chloride does not conduct electricity as a solid but does when dissolved in water. Include the process of dissolution and electrolysis.
mark_scheme: Solid NaCl: ions held in fixed positions in lattice — cannot move to carry charge (1); dissolution: water molecules surround and pull apart Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions — lattice breaks down (1); aqueous ions free to move — solution conducts electricity (1); electrolysis: when current applied, Na⁺ moves to cathode (−), Cl⁻ moves to anode (+) (1); at cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (reduction) — though in water, H₂ produced preferentially (1); at anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation) — chlorine gas produced (1).

question: Evaluate the properties of different types of steel (mild steel, stainless steel, high carbon steel) and explain how their composition relates to their uses.
mark_scheme: Mild steel: low carbon content (~0.2%) — malleable, easily shaped; used in car bodies, buildings (1); high carbon steel: more carbon — harder, more brittle; used in cutting tools, blades (1); stainless steel: contains chromium (~18%) and nickel — resists corrosion (1); chromium forms thin oxide layer on surface — prevents rusting (1); all harder than pure iron — alloying atoms disrupt regular lattice, prevent layer sliding (1); choice of steel determined by required balance of strength, hardness, flexibility and corrosion resistance (1).

question: Explain the properties of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes, and evaluate their potential uses in medicine and technology.
mark_scheme: Fullerenes: closed carbon structures — C₆₀ sphere (buckminsterfullerene) or cylindrical nanotubes (1); nanotubes: very high length-to-diameter ratio — extremely strong and conduct electricity (1); medical use: drug delivery — C₆₀ can be functionalised to carry drug molecules to cancer cells specifically (1); reduces side effects compared to conventional chemotherapy (1); technology: carbon nanotube composites — lightweight but stronger than steel for aerospace/sports equipment (1); nanoelectronics: transistors from nanotubes could be much smaller than silicon — faster computers (1).

question: Describe the three types of strong chemical bonding (ionic, covalent, metallic). For each, describe the bonding model and explain one property that arises from it.
mark_scheme: Ionic: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1); high melting point — large amount of energy needed to break many strong electrostatic forces (1); Covalent: electrons shared between non-metal atoms — strong bonds within molecules (1); simple molecular substances have low boiling points because intermolecular forces between molecules are weak (1); Metallic: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (1); good electrical conductivity — delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge (1).

question: A student claims that all substances with high melting points must have ionic bonds. Evaluate this claim using evidence from different types of bonding and structure.
mark_scheme: Claim is incorrect — there are other reasons for high melting point (1); giant covalent structures also have very high melting points: diamond (~3550°C), SiO₂ (~1610°C) — due to many strong covalent bonds to break (1); metals also have high melting points: tungsten (~3400°C) — due to strong metallic bonding (1); ionic compounds vary: NaCl (801°C), MgO (2852°C) depending on charge and ion size (1); simple molecular covalent substances have LOW melting points despite having strong covalent bonds (1); conclusion: melting point depends on type of bonding AND structure — cannot determine bonding type from melting point alone (1).

question: Describe what is meant by a giant ionic lattice and explain how the arrangement of ions relates to the properties of sodium chloride.
mark_scheme: Giant ionic lattice: regular 3D arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions (1); each Na⁺ surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ ions and vice versa (1); strong electrostatic forces in all directions — high melting point (1); lattice extends throughout whole crystal — brittle (layers of same charge repel when shifted) (1); dissolves in water — polar water molecules attract and surround individual ions (1).

question: State what type of bonding is present in sodium chloride and in oxygen gas.
mark_scheme: Sodium chloride has ionic bonding (1); oxygen gas has covalent bonding (1).

question: Explain why pure metals are less hard than alloys.
mark_scheme: In a pure metal, all atoms are the same size and the layers can slide over each other easily (1); in an alloy, different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice, preventing layers from sliding so the alloy is harder (1).

question: Give two uses of nanoparticles and explain why their large surface area makes them effective.
mark_scheme: Any two uses: e.g. catalysts, antibacterial coatings, drug delivery, sun cream (1); large surface area means more active sites available, making them more reactive or effective at low quantities (1).

question: State two properties of giant covalent structures and explain why they have these properties.
mark_scheme: Very high melting point because many strong covalent bonds must be broken (1); they do not conduct electricity (except graphite) because there are no free electrons or ions (1).

question: Explain why ionic compounds are brittle.
mark_scheme: When a force is applied, layers of ions shift so that ions of the same charge are next to each other (1); like charges repel causing the crystal to shatter / crack (1).

question: Give two examples of alloys and state what they are made from.
mark_scheme: Any two from: steel — iron and carbon (1); brass — copper and zinc (1); bronze — copper and tin (1); solder — tin and lead (1).

question: Compare the electrical conductivity of diamond and graphite. Explain the difference.
mark_scheme: Diamond does not conduct electricity; graphite does conduct electricity (1); diamond has no free electrons; graphite has one delocalised electron per carbon atom that can carry charge (1).

question: Explain how an ionic bond is formed between magnesium and oxygen. Include the charges of the ions formed.
mark_scheme: Magnesium is a metal and loses 2 electrons to form a Mg²⁺ ion (1); oxygen is a non-metal and gains 2 electrons to form an O²⁻ ion (1); the oppositely charged ions are attracted to each other by electrostatic forces — forming an ionic bond (1).

question: Describe the structure of an ionic compound and explain why it cannot conduct electricity when solid.
mark_scheme: Ionic compounds form a giant ionic lattice — regular 3D arrangement of oppositely charged ions (1); held together by strong electrostatic forces (1); when solid, the ions are held in fixed positions and cannot move to carry electrical charge (1).

question: Explain why simple molecular substances have low melting points even though the covalent bonds within molecules are strong.
mark_scheme: Simple molecular substances have strong covalent bonds within each molecule (1); however, only weak intermolecular forces exist between molecules (1); it is the weak intermolecular forces — not the covalent bonds — that are broken during melting, so little energy is required (1).

question: Describe the structure of a metal and explain why metals are good conductors of both electricity and heat.
mark_scheme: Metals consist of a giant lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons (1); delocalised electrons carry electrical charge so metals conduct electricity (1); delocalised electrons also transfer kinetic energy through the lattice — metals conduct heat (1).

question: Explain why nanoparticles have different properties from the bulk material, and give one potential risk of their use.
mark_scheme: Nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio (1); this gives them different chemical and physical properties compared to larger particles of the same material (1); potential risk: unknown long-term health effects — nanoparticles may be inhaled and enter cells, causing damage (1).

question: Describe the structure of graphite and explain why it is soft and slippery.
mark_scheme: Graphite consists of layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings (1); each carbon atom is bonded to three others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom (1); the layers are held together by weak intermolecular forces and can slide over each other easily, making graphite soft and useful as a lubricant (1).

question: Explain what is meant by metallic bonding and how this gives metals their characteristic properties.
mark_scheme: Metallic bonding involves a giant lattice of positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons (1); the strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and delocalised electrons holds the structure together (1); the delocalised electrons allow metals to conduct electricity and heat; the ability of layers to slide gives metals their malleability and ductility (1).

question: Compare the electrical conductivity of an ionic compound when solid and when dissolved in water.
mark_scheme: When solid: ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move — does not conduct electricity (1); when dissolved in water: the lattice breaks apart and ions become free to move (1); the movement of charged ions allows an electrical current to flow — conducts electricity (1).

question: Describe why alloys are harder than the pure metals they are made from.
mark_scheme: Pure metals have a regular arrangement of identical-sized atoms — layers can slide over each other easily (1); in alloys, atoms of different sizes are mixed in the lattice (1); the different-sized atoms distort the regular arrangement making it harder for layers to slide — the alloy is harder and stronger (1).

question: Explain why diamond is used as a cutting tool.
mark_scheme: Diamond has a giant covalent structure in which each carbon atom is bonded to four others (1); the many strong covalent bonds make diamond extremely hard (1); this hardness means it can cut through most other materials, making it suitable for use in drill bits and cutting tools (1).

question: Describe what fullerenes are and give one use of buckminsterfullerene.
mark_scheme: Fullerenes are molecules made entirely of carbon atoms arranged in hollow spheres or tubes (1); buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) consists of 60 carbon atoms arranged in a sphere (1); one use: drug delivery — the hollow cage can carry drug molecules to specific target cells in the body (1).

question: Compare ionic and covalent bonding in terms of the particles involved and how the bond is formed.
mark_scheme: Ionic bonding: involves a metal and a non-metal; electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction (1); covalent bonding: involves two non-metals; electrons are shared between the atoms so both achieve a full outer shell (1); ionic compounds form giant lattice structures; covalent compounds can be simple molecular or giant covalent (1).

question: State the type of polymerisation used to make poly(propene) from propene.
mark_scheme: Addition polymerisation (1).

question: State one property of polymers that makes them useful for food packaging and one environmental disadvantage of this use.
mark_scheme: Property: waterproof / flexible / lightweight / cheap (1); disadvantage: non-biodegradable so persists in landfill / oceans for hundreds of years (1).

question: Explain why most addition polymers are non-biodegradable.
mark_scheme: They are made of very long carbon chains (1); microorganisms do not have enzymes to break down these C–C bonds / the polymer backbone (1).

question: Compare the monomers and products of addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation.
mark_scheme: Addition: monomers contain a C=C double bond; only one product — the polymer (1); condensation: monomers have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH); two products formed — the polymer and a small molecule (water) (1); example of each: e.g. poly(ethene) from ethene (addition); nylon from diamine and dicarboxylic acid (condensation) (1).
